domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is Anti-gravity, an agent-first IDE for software engineering with codegen, agent-managed coding workflows, and IDE-integrated agents. Anti-gravity is a coding assistant IDE built on a developer platform for software builders. The product is launched and in active deployment with an internal research-product flywheel driving iteration. The content is accessible to practitioners familiar with IDEs and agents but assumes working knowledge of model capabilities and agent architecture. This is a conference talk from the AI Engineer Summit. All evidence is sourced directly from the transcript with said_in_transcript grade.

summary: Kevin Hou leads product engineering for Google Anti-gravity, a new IDE from Google DeepMind launched with Gemini 3 Pro. The product is built on three surfaces: an editor (forked VS Code with autocomplete and agent sidebar), an agent-controlled Chrome browser, and an agent manager as the central hub. The paradigm shift places agents outside the IDE, operating across multiple surfaces. The agent manager provides a higher-level view than diffs, with an inbox for managing multiple agents and OS-level notifications for multi-threading across tasks. Users can switch between editor and agent manager in under 100 milliseconds via command-E/control-E. The agent-controlled browser offers context retrieval using the user's authentication for services like Google Docs and GitHub dashboards, and verification through screen recordings showing the agent's mouse movements and actions. Hou emphasizes that product paradigms follow model capability step functions: autocomplete, then chat, then agents, and now this new paradigm. Four improvement categories drove the design: intelligence/reasoning, nuanced tool use, longer-running tasks, and multimodality. Building on these capabilities, Anti-gravity introduces 'artifacts'—dynamic, multimodal representations the agent generates to organize its work, communicate with users, and share information across agents and memory. Artifacts include implementation plans (like PRDs with open questions), task lists, architecture diagrams, walkthroughs, images, screen recordings, and mermaid diagrams. The model dynamically decides whether and what type of artifact to generate. The artifact system enables Google Docs- and GitHub-style commenting in both text and image space, allowing users to provide feedback mid-execution without interrupting the agent's task loop. Artifacts can be stored in memory for future reuse, such as API schema research. The agent manager is optimized as an artifact review system supporting parallelism and orchestration across multiple projects or sub-tasks. An editor escape hatch remains available for tasks requiring manual intervention to get from 80% to 100%. DeepMind's embedded research collaboration gave the team early Gemini access to identify strengths and gaps, forming a research-product flywheel. Internal Google engineers and DeepMind researchers use Anti-gravity daily, providing real-world signal on model gaps that evals cannot reveal. Two concrete flywheel examples: computer use gaps were identified collaboratively across product and research teams (data distribution mismatches, agent harness issues), and artifacts required training and data distribution work with research teams to improve from poor initial performance to strong Gemini 3 Pro capability. Hou frames the three-step process as: pushing the ceiling of agent ambition (including vibe coding), building the agent-first experience (artifacts, agent manager), and leveraging the research-product flywheel. He thanks the AI Engineer Summit and invites community feedback.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Intro & Anti-gravity Launch
sections.summary: Hou introduces Anti-gravity, launched alongside Gemini 3 Pro, as the first IDE from a foundational lab. He notes it is unapologetically agent-first and outlines the talk will cover what was built and the philosophy behind it.

sections.title: Anti-gravity Product Overview (Three Surfaces)
sections.summary: Anti-gravity has three surfaces: editor, browser, and agent manager. The paradigm shift is agents living outside the IDE across multiple surfaces. The agent manager is the central hub, one level above diffs.

sections.title: Agent Manager & Editor Integration
sections.summary: The editor is forked VS Code with autocomplete and agent sidebar mirrored with the agent manager. Users can switch between surfaces in under 100ms. The agent manager has an inbox for managing multiple agents and OS-level notifications.

sections.title: Agent-Controlled Browser & Context Retrieval
sections.summary: The agent-controlled Chrome browser provides authenticated context retrieval and the ability to take control, click, scroll, and run JavaScript. Screen recordings provide verifiable results. The agent manager serves as control panel with editor and browser as tools.

sections.title: Philosophy: Model Capabilities Driving Product Paradigms
sections.summary: Hou explains product paradigms follow model capability step functions: autocomplete, chat, agents. DeepMind embedding gave early Gemini access to identify strengths and gaps. Four improvement categories: intelligence, tool use, longer-running tasks, multimodality.

sections.title: Four Categories of Improvements & Browser Use
sections.summary: Details four improvement categories with visual aids. Browser use is highlighted as a major unlock for both retrieval and verification, addressing context richness beyond code—what to build, how to build it, and building it.

sections.title: Computer Use & Visual Verification
sections.summary: Demonstrates computer use with a flight tracker app showing the agent controlling the browser, clicking, scrolling, and retrieving DOM. Screen recordings replace diffs as verification, and the model can iterate using multimodal image understanding. Transitions to image generation as the second focus area.

sections.title: Image Generation & Design Iteration
sections.summary: Hou demonstrates mockups in image space, showing how users can comment on designs and the agent applies those comments. Image generation (Nano Banana Pro) was available on day one, making Anti-gravity a place where any new model capability can be represented in the product.

sections.title: The Artifacts Interaction Pattern
sections.summary: Introduces artifacts as a new interaction pattern necessitated by longer-running, more capable agents. Artifacts are dynamic representations the agent generates for self-organization, user communication (screenshots, recordings), and cross-agent sharing or memory. The agent manager dedicates half the screen to artifacts, replacing hard-to-follow chain-of-thought token streams with visual representations.

sections.title: Artifacts Types & Dynamic Generation
sections.summary: The model dynamically decides whether to produce an artifact and what type. Common types include markdown plans (like PRDs with open questions), task lists, architecture diagrams, walkthroughs, images, screen recordings, and mermaid diagrams. The model can auto-continue if it has no open questions, or surface questions for user feedback before proceeding.

sections.title: Artifacts for Memory, Notifications, & Feedback
sections.summary: Artifacts are explained with purpose, audience (sub-agents, other conversations, memory bank), and notifications for open questions. API schema research is stored in memory for reuse. Google Docs- and GitHub-inspired commenting works in both text and image space (Figma-style highlight), enabling mid-execution feedback without interrupting the agent's task loop.

sections.title: Parallelism, Orchestration & Editor Escape Hatch
sections.summary: The agent manager handles parallelism and orchestration across projects and sub-tasks, with artifacts providing feedback and notifications signaling attention needs. An editor escape hatch via command-E opens the exact files, artifacts, and conversation for manual autocomplete or synchronous chat to get from 80% to 100%.

sections.title: Research-Product Flywheel (Start)
sections.summary: Hou transitions to discussing what happens under the hood at DeepMind, referencing a lesson learned from three years in codegen, setting up the research-product flywheel discussion.

sections.title: Research-Product Flywheel & Closing Remarks
sections.summary: Hou details the research-product flywheel: internal Google engineers and DeepMind researchers use Anti-gravity daily, surfacing real model gaps that evals cannot. Two examples: computer use gaps identified collaboratively across teams (data distribution mismatches, agent harness issues), and artifacts requiring training and data distribution work with research teams to reach strong Gemini 3 Pro performance. Hou frames the three-step process: push the agent ambition ceiling (including vibe coding), build agent-first experiences (artifacts, agent manager), and leverage the flywheel. He thanks AI Engineer Summit organizers Swix and Ben, invites community feedback via Twitter DMs, and humorously suggests adopting a TPU to help reduce pager duty.

evidence.excerpt: Anti-gravity, notably anti-gravity, not anti-gravity. Anti-gravity. It's an AI developer platform with three surfaces.
command E or control E and hop instantly from the editor into the agent manager and vice versa. And this takes on under 100 milliseconds.
The product is only ever as good as the models that power it... every single one of these product paradigms is sort of motivated by some change that happens with model capabilities.
there are four main categories of improvements... the first one is intelligence and reasoning... longer running tasks... and then multimodal.

you end up with not just a diff, you end up with a screen recording of what it did... the model can take this and because it has the ability to understand images, it can take this and iterate from there.
we're calling this artifacts. This is a new way to work with an agent. And this is one of my favorite parts about the product. And at its core is this agent manager.

what's really awesome is that the model will decide whether or not it can auto continue. If it has no questions, why should it wait?
